title: How to be a guest
hook: seven weeks visiting seven doors, one first idea at a time, in each tradition's own words

segments.voice: Yesterday, camp four closed with the reed and the emperor. Your line was longing and duty. Day two hundred thirty-two, and camp five begins.

Everyone pauses before eating, and you're not sure whether to bow your head. There's a word everyone knows but you. You take your shoes off only after noticing everyone else's by the door. That's being a guest at a friend's family dinner, a different family from yours. Being a good guest is a skill, and most of us learned it by accident. For the next seven weeks, the job is to be a guest on purpose, at seven doors. Today, silverware.
screen: `SOMEONE ELSE'S FAMILY DINNER.` → `THE SHOES BY THE DOOR.` → `HOW TO BE A GUEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the plan. Seven weeks, seven visits: Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, Christianity, the Catholic tradition, Islam and Sikhism. Each is a whole door on this app, with years of its own lessons. One week in each, one first idea a day, the way someone at home in that tradition might first explain it to a friend. That's all it is: a visit. So, four house rules. First, use their words. Hindus say dharma, Jews say Torah, Muslims say the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, Sikhs say Guru Nanak. Learn the words the way the family says them, not translated into something more comfortable. Second, a visit is not a conversion and not a comparison. Nobody is being recruited, and nobody is being ranked. When an idea sounds like something from another door, let each keep its own meaning, the way Rumi and Marcus were kept apart. Third, where a family disagrees with itself, say so. Every tradition has schools and arguments; name who says what rather than pick a side. Fourth, don't pocket the silverware. It's easy to take a practice home, a candle, a chant, a bow, and strip away what it means. Try things if you like, as a guest, and remember whose table you're at. There's an old line from the Taittiriya Upanishad, a Hindu scripture, often recited in India: let the guest be as God to you. That's a host's duty. The guest's half of the bargain is to be worthy of it.
screen: `SEVEN DOORS, ONE WEEK EACH.` · `USE THEIR WORDS.` · `NOT A CONVERSION, NOT A CONTEST.` · `DON'T POCKET THE SILVERWARE.` · then, large: `A GUEST, RESPECTFUL.`

segments.voice: Remember a time someone was a wonderful guest in your home, or a time you felt truly welcomed in someone else's. What did they do: listen more than talk, ask before touching things, say thank you in the right way? Choose one simple thing you'll bring to these seven visits.
Silverware. Try a practice as a guest if you like, but don't pocket the silverware: remember whose table you're at. Today's word.
Your line: a guest, respectful. A good guest listens first. See you at the first door.

howItsDone: Visitors to temples, gurdwaras, mosques, synagogues and churches usually learn the house customs first: shoes, head coverings, dress, silence, and asking before taking photographs.
